wachiman.text:
canManage() grants manage to admins that only have VIEW on all groups

`canManage()` returns true when `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)` matches, so an all-groups permission with only the `view` scope passes `requireManage()`. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` (GroupsResource.java:181) uses only `auth.groups().requireManage()`, which means a view-only admin can create top-level groups and move existing groups to the top level. The interface Javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator.java:72-77) repeats the same VIEW/MANAGE wording. Change the check to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, the same as `canManage(GroupModel)` at line 79, and add a test that a VIEW-only all-groups admin gets 403 on POST /groups.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs, not group IDs

In V2, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` creates the resource with name = group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:109,121). Its `getId()` is a generated authz UUID. This loop passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission`, which looks the resource up with `findByName` (line 141). It also adds `getId()` to the result set. So the lookup never finds the group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource, and the returned IDs are not group IDs. V1 uses `resource.getName()` here (GroupPermissions.java:315).

Callers pass this set as the group filter to `UsersResource.getUsersCount` (UsersResource.java:398,425,430) and set it as `UserModel.GROUPS` for the search (UsersResource.java:448-450, BruteForceUsersResource.java:147-149). An admin who can see users only through group view-members gets a wrong count, or an empty or wrong search result, with no error. Use `groupResource.getName()` in both places.

I could not confirm that `findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` returns the per-group resources. `create(server, name, owner)` does not appear to set a type. If it doesn't, this method always returns an empty set, and the count endpoint is wrong either way. The tests only cover the list endpoint, where `toRepresentation` filters each user with `canView` again.

requireManageMembers Javadoc points to the wrong method

The Javadoc for `requireManageMembers` says it throws when `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` is false. It should name `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. Also, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`'s `@return` (line 145) says "Stream", but the method returns a `Set`.

Two providers with the same order are now picked silently, which can mean a non-FIPS provider in a FIPS setup

Before this change, finding more than one CryptoProvider threw an IllegalStateException. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first one is used. The only trace of the others is a debug log (lines 64-70). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so when two of them are on the classpath together the stable sort leaves them in ServiceLoader (classpath) order. That is the same misconfiguration that used to fail at startup. In a FIPS deployment that accidentally ships crypto-default, the server can now start on the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider without any visible warning. This affects every caller that relies on detection: `KeycloakApplication` (services/.../KeycloakApplication.java:89) and admin-cli `Globals` (Globals.java:44). Quarkus is not affected because it calls `setProvider` explicitly. Suggested fix: still throw when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, so only the authz-client fallback (100) can lose quietly. Logging the ignored providers at warn level would also help.

Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 build two `ASN1Encoder` instances and throw them away. Lines 119-120 build the same values again. You can delete the two lines.

Test only round-trips through the new code and never checks the DER against the JDK

The test decodes the JDK signature, re-encodes it with the new `ASN1Encoder` and decodes it again with the new `ASN1Decoder`. If the encoder and decoder share the same mistake, the test still passes. Call `Signature.initVerify(publicKey)` and `verify(asn1Des)` (or compare `asn1Des` with `sign`), which checks the produced DER against the JDK. Also, one default `KeyPairGenerator("EC")` key (P-256 or P-384, depending on the JDK) is used for all three algorithms. So ES512 never runs with a P-521 key, where r and s are 66 bytes and can carry a leading sign byte, which is the case the padding and truncation in `integerToBytes` exist for. Generating a key on the matching curve for each algorithm would cover it.

getSubGroupsCount now returns null, but the SPI says it never does

`GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is documented as "Never returns {@code null}" (server-spi/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/GroupModel.java:296). This change returns `null` when the group was deleted from the database while its cached copy was still in use. In this repository the only caller is `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90). It passes the value to `setSubGroupCount(Long)`, so nothing breaks today. Extensions that rely on the documented contract and unbox the value would throw a new NPE instead. The cached adapter's other lazy loaders return an empty fallback when the group is gone (`Collections::emptySet` and `MultivaluedHashMap::new` in CachedGroup.java:55-57). Returning `0L` would match that and keep the contract. Otherwise, update the javadoc.

Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can miss the failure it tests for

Right after `deletedAll.set(true)`, the test checks `caughtExceptions` (line 157) without waiting for the reader thread. A request that is still running, which is exactly the one most likely to hit the concurrent delete, can add its exception after the check has passed. Nothing requires the reader to run at all either: if the 100 deletes finish before the thread's first request, the test passes without exercising the race. The thread also outlives the test. Keep a reference to the `Thread` and `join()` it before the assertion. Also consider waiting until at least one read has finished (a counter or latch) before you start deleting.

Call to `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments won't compile

The only declaration is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160. Nothing in services declares a no-argument overload, and a grep for `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(` finds only these four places. So `services` fails to compile. Even if you just pass `context.getUser()`, the check is still wrong, because of the inverted condition reported in the next finding.

Passkey conditional UI is now only set up when a user is already set, so a normal first login loses passkeys

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns `... && user != null`. Before this change, `fillContextForm` ran exactly when the user was *not* yet identified: in the `else` branch of `authenticate`, and in `challenge` behind `context.getUser() == null`.

Now, on a fresh login (`context.getUser()` is null at line 115), `fillContextForm` is never called. The login page then has no WebAuthn challenge or `webauth` form, and passkey login is impossible. The new tests themselves expect `//form[@id='webauth']` on the first login page (PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.java:196, :238), so they would fail.

The same applies to the error path at line 137: when the username is unknown, the user stays null and the passkey data is dropped. The PR's goal of also enabling passkeys during re-authentication needs the check to be just `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`, without the user condition. Re-authentication with a passkey is still safe without it: `WebAuthnAuthenticator.action` rejects a different user (WebAuthnAuthenticator.java:201-209), and `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` returns false, so no credential list is leaked.

Missing `@Override` on `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators`

This method overrides `WebAuthnAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` (WebAuthnAuthenticator.java:128), but it has no `@Override`. If the base method is ever renamed, this override would silently stop applying, and the form would start listing the user's credentials during conditional login.

Test name says the user has no passkey, but the test disables passkeys for the whole realm

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`. That means it never covers the case its name and the comment at line 304 describe: passkeys enabled for the realm, re-authenticating a user who has no passkey. Under the intended behaviour, that user would still see the conditional passkey UI. Either rename the test or add the realm-enabled case.

Separately, the `try { findElement(...); fail(...) } catch (Exception)` pattern at lines 291-296 and 312-317 only works because `AssertionError` is not an `Exception`. `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)`, as used in the organization test, would be clearer.

A hung flusher process is never killed, so its replacement runs alongside it on the same shards

Processes are made with `self.mp_context.Process`, where `mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` (lines 53, 105). That gives a `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. In CPython, `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess` directly, not `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `process.kill()` never runs.

The old code called `self.process.kill()` with no condition. Now, in the `hang` case (line 236), the stuck process stays alive. `_create_process_for_shards` then starts a second process for the same shards (line 259), and both call `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` on the same Redis queues. That can produce the same segments twice. The stuck process is also leaked, and this repeats on every restart, up to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`.

The same check in `join` (line 346) means `terminate()` never runs either. Fix: check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

join() stops looping once the deadline passes and skips the remaining processes

When the deadline has passed, `break` leaves the loop. `terminate()` (line 347) never runs for that process or any process after it. The old code always terminated after the wait. Those processes are only stopped by the `stopped` flag, so a process that is stuck in Redis or Kafka keeps running past `join`. Use `continue`, or skip only the wait and still terminate each process (once the isinstance check at line 346 is fixed too).

`spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` now applies per process, not per consumer

`flush_segments` caps each shard at `ceil(max_flush_segments / len(self.assigned_shards))` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:382-384). Each per-process buffer now holds only its own shards, so each process can flush up to `max_flush_segments` per cycle. The whole consumer can flush `num_processes × max_flush_segments`. If the option is meant as a consumer-wide limit, divide it by `num_processes`, or document the new meaning.

Cluster memory is queried once per process buffer on every submit

`get_memory_info` returns `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)` for the whole Redis cluster (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:375-376), whatever the buffer's shards. Calling it for every buffer repeats the same INFO queries N times. `used` and `available` are each multiplied by N, so the ratio does not change. One call is enough, for example `next(iter(self.buffers.values())).get_memory_info()`.

Inconsistent metric tag key: `shards` here, `shard` elsewhere

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards`. The `produce` timer (line 185) and `segment_size_bytes` (line 195) use `shard`, so dashboards can't group these metrics by one key. Also, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list, so the number of distinct tag values grows with the shard combinations.

Dead code: `_create_process_for_shard` and `if not process`

Nothing calls `_create_process_for_shard`. `if not process: continue` (line 222) never fires, because Thread and Process objects are always truthy. Remove both.

Docstring says one process per shard, but the CLI default is 1 process

The CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1 (src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:434). Shards are spread round-robin over `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes (lines 60-66). Only when `max_processes` is None do you get one process per shard.

`time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing because the test patched `time.sleep`

Line 15 sets `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`. Since the test calls it as `time.sleep`, the patched version runs, so line 62 doesn't wait. The comment "Give flusher threads time to process" is false. Whether the flush happens before `join` sets `stopped` still depends on thread timing. To make this deterministic, poll until `messages` is non-empty, with a real deadline, e.g. a saved reference to the original sleep.

zip(error_ids, events.values()) pairs error IDs with the wrong events

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` (src/sentry/nodestore/base.py:174-209) removes duplicate ids, puts the uncached results first, and then appends cached hits with `items.update(cache_items)`. So `events.values()` is not in `error_ids` order once some ids are cached. It is also shorter than `error_ids` when there are duplicates. When that happens, `zip` gives an event's title, message and timestamp to a different error ID, and Seer receives the mismatched data. Nothing fails or logs. The fix is to look each one up by key: `data = events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id=eid))` for each `eid` in `error_ids`.

Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` from the error event's nodestore payload, which is a float in seconds. `gen_request_data` compares it with the top-level `timestamp` of each replay recording event, which rrweb stores in epoch milliseconds (`event_parser.py:182` passes it into the log text unchanged). A seconds value is always smaller than a milliseconds value, so every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb. The log Seer receives then also mixes the two units in its `at {timestamp}` text. The summary is told errors happened at the start of the session, and nothing reports the problem. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (`* 1000`) before sorting and comparing.

Assemble analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` check. Requests that the endpoint then rejects are still counted as assemble events, which inflates the metric. Consider moving the call after the feature check, or after the request has been validated.

One invalid report drops the whole batch

If any report in the array fails validation, the endpoint returns 422 and none of the valid reports in the same POST are counted. Browsers batch reports from different pages, and the endpoint accepts report types it does not control, so one malformed entry loses every report sent with it. Consider skipping and logging the invalid entries and processing the rest.

age/timestamp mutual-exclusion check is skipped when either value is 0

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check truthiness: `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A report with `age: 0` and a timestamp, or with `timestamp: 0` and an age, passes both checks even though it has both fields. A report with neither field also passes, because both fields are `required=False`. Consider checking `"age" in self.initial_data` instead, and requiring exactly one of the two fields in `validate()`.

Flag-gated TableWidgetVisualization always renders empty

With `use-table-widget-visualization` enabled, every table widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and empty `data`. `result.data`, `result.meta` and `fields` are all ignored, so any organization with the flag sees blank tables. If this is meant as scaffolding, consider passing the real result data through before the flag is turned on for anyone.

Attribute keys query lost retry:false / staleTime:0 / refetchOnWindowFocus:false and the environment filter

The old `useApiQuery` call set `retry: false`, `staleTime: 0` and `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`. The new `useQuery` uses none of them, so it falls back to the app's QueryClient defaults. If those defaults include retries, a failing attributes endpoint now gets retried, and `isLoading` (which is now `isFetching`) stays true longer while that happens. The query also used to send `selection.environments`; `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` leaves it out on purpose (useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys.tsx:50). That means the key list no longer narrows by the selected environment. Please confirm both changes are intended. If not, add the old options back to `useQuery`.

Custom renderer results that are falsy get replaced by the default

Both renderers fall back to the default with `if (cell)` (lines 32 and 71). The documented contract is that only `undefined` means "use the fallback", so a custom renderer that returns `0`, `''` or `null` on purpose gets overwritten by the default cell. Check `cell !== undefined` instead.

Story copy typo and missing spaces "the the most basic example" repeats "the". There is no space before `tableData` (line 28), and there are similar gaps around `TabularData` (line 58) and `renderTableBodyCell` (line 111), so the rendered text runs words together, e.g. "requirestableData".

"Project not found" can show while projects are still loading

`useProjectFromId` (static/app/utils/useProjectFromId.tsx:7-12) looks the id up in `useProjects().projects` and ignores the `fetching` state. Line 90 therefore shows the error alert any time the project list doesn't contain the replay's project yet. That includes the moment before the projects store has loaded, so the user sees a 'Project not found' error flash before the summary loads. Consider also reading `fetching` from `useProjects()` and showing the loading state until it finishes.

Tests use second-based breadcrumb timestamps, so they hide a seconds-vs-milliseconds mixup when errors are interleaved

`gen_request_data` (src/sentry/replays/endpoints/project_replay_summarize_breadcrumbs.py:153-155) compares `error_events[i]["timestamp"]` with the recording event's top-level `timestamp`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data (`data.get("timestamp")`, line 115), which is in epoch seconds. The top-level `timestamp` on an rrweb recording event is in epoch milliseconds. These tests use seconds for the breadcrumbs (`1.5`/`2.0` here, and `float(now.timestamp())` at lines 188 and 254), so the interleaving looks correct. With real recordings, every error timestamp is about 1000× smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb. Their `at ...` values are then in a different unit from the breadcrumbs' values. The summary sent to Seer comes out in the wrong order, and nothing reports it. Please build the fixtures with millisecond breadcrumb timestamps, as real segments have, and convert one side in `gen_request_data` (for example, multiply the error timestamp by 1000) so the ordering assertion tests the real case.

OptimizedCursorPaginator can't page a datetime key, so the optimized audit-log path returns 500

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` copies the integer `Paginator.get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor`. The audit-log endpoint uses it with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py:80).

- **Item key:** `getattr(item, "datetime")` is a `datetime`, so `math.ceil(value)` raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key on the results (line 904), so any `?optimized_pagination=true` request that returns at least one row fails with a 500.
- **Cursor value:** `value_from_cursor` returns the raw millisecond integer. `build_queryset` then emits `datetime <= <int>`, comparing a timestamp column with an integer.

`DateTimePaginator` (paginator.py:230-241) converts in both directions. Subclass `DateTimePaginator` or reuse its key and value methods, and add a test that exercises this path.

The negative-offset "advanced feature" can't work: Django querysets reject negative slices

Cursor offsets come straight from the client (`Cursor.from_string`, cursors.py:59), so `cursor=0:-5:0` reaches line 882 as `queryset[-5:...]`. Django `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for that.

This is not a `BadPaginationError`, so `paginate` (base.py:540) does not turn it into a 400; the request fails with a 500. The comment's claims are false: the ORM does not "handle negative slicing automatically", and nothing gives "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds".

Remove this branch, or reject negative offsets with a `BadPaginationError`.

BasePaginator only clamps negative offsets on next-page cursors; prev cursors still crash

This change to the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` affects every subclass (`Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and others).

- **Next cursors:** a negative offset is clamped to 0.
- **Prev cursors:** a negative offset is passed through unchanged. A client-supplied cursor such as `1:-1:1` still raises Django's negative-indexing `ValueError` and returns a 500.
- **Unchanged check:** line 192 still compares against `offset`, not `start_offset`.

The comment says negative offsets are allowed and "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions"; neither is true. Clamp in both directions, or raise `BadPaginationError` for `offset < 0`, so a malformed cursor gets a 400.

The gate is not an admin check: has_global_access is open-membership access, and is_superuser skips active-superuser checks

The comment says the path is for "authorized administrators". It isn't restricted that way:

- **`member.has_global_access`:** any member of an org with open membership has it. It is not an admin role.
- **`request.user.is_superuser`:** Sentry elsewhere uses `is_active_superuser(request)`, which also requires an active superuser session. The bare flag skips that.

The queryset is already scoped to the organization, so no data crosses orgs today. If the path really needs a privilege gate, use the existing helpers. If it doesn't, drop the gate and the comment.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result and the docstring claims features it doesn't have

Apart from the broken negative-offset branch, `get_result` (lines 845-911) is a copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. There is no "optimized query path" and no "streamlined boundary handling".

The comment added in cursors.py:26-27 is also wrong: the `Cursor` constructor has always accepted any integer offset, so the change there is comment-only. Once the datetime and negative-slice bugs are fixed, the class adds nothing over `DateTimePaginator`; consider removing it and the query flag.

New TotalDocs() log call reads the bleve cache map with no lock while the event goroutine can write to it

`TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-149) loops over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. This line calls it after the watch-event goroutine has already started (search.go:207-213). That goroutine's `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex` writes `b.cache[key]` (bleve.go:137-139). A write event for a namespace/resource that has no index yet, arriving during startup, can therefore hit a concurrent map read and write. In Go that is a fatal runtime error which crashes the process, not a panic you can recover. The metrics collector (bleve_index_metrics.go:96) has the same unlocked read. Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` inside `TotalDocs`.

Requests are no longer refused after Stop()

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped" (lines 321, 328, 339). Before this change, every RPC called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned that `initErr` once `once` had fired, so requests after shutdown failed with a clear error. This PR removes those calls from Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob and GetBlob, and nothing reads `initErr` any more. During shutdown, requests now run against a backend whose lifecycle `Stop` has already run and whose `s.ctx` has been cancelled. IsHealthy also keeps reporting through diagnostics as if nothing happened. Fix: keep a cheap check of the stopped state (for example an atomic flag or reading `initErr`) at the top of the RPCs, or delete the now-dead `initErr` assignments in Stop if serving after Stop is intended.

Narrower lock lets two builds of the same key run at once

`BuildIndex` used to hold `cacheMu` for the whole build, which serialized builds. Now only the map write is locked. Two `getOrCreateIndex` calls for the same key (the Search path and handleEvent) can both see a nil index and build at the same time. Each lists the whole resource, and the last write to `cache[key]` wins: the losing index is dropped, along with any events written into it while it was cached. For file-based indexes, both calls run `bleve.New` on the same directory. The TODO at search.go:288-290 already notes that a per-key guard is needed. A per-key singleflight would keep the parallel startup builds without duplicating work.

Parallel init workers now write shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` at the same time

Each errgroup closure assigns the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed`, with no synchronization. Now that `BuildIndex` no longer serializes on `cacheMu`, builds really overlap, so these are data races; `go test -race` will flag them. `totalBatchesIndexed` can also come out too low. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Is the postgres skip hiding a regression from the eager Init?

This PR makes `NewResourceServer` run `Init` right away: lifecycle init, a full search index build and the watcher (server.go:258). Before, Init ran lazily on the first request. The storage-server target now does that work inside `service.start` (sql/service.go:113). Did the postgres failure in Drone start with this change? If it did, skipping the test hides a startup problem (timeout or ordering) rather than a CI quirk. Please link a tracking issue for the TODO.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now inherits from `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. It leaves `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` unimplemented, and all four are `@abc.abstractmethod` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py:142-170). `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points to this class (grouptype.py:27), and `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates it with `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (models/detector.py:86). So any `metric_alert_fire` detector now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` the moment its handler is read. That aborts `process_detectors` for every detector in the batch. Before this change the handler returned `[]`. A search found no production caller of `process_detectors` yet, so this does not block the merge, but it is wrong as written. Either keep a concrete stub (implement the four members, returning empty or no-op values, with a TODO) or leave it on `DetectorHandler` until the real implementation lands. The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector` comment on line 10 is also stale now.

Occurrence assertions only compare the hard-coded id, so they verify almost nothing

`IssueOccurrence.__eq__` compares only `id` (src/sentry/issues/issue_occurrence.py:181-184). `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` always uses the same id (`eb4b0acf...`), so every `== DetectorEvaluationResult(..., result=occurrence, ...)` assertion passes no matter what fingerprint, type or priority the handler produced. This already hides a mistake in this diff: `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` builds the expected occurrence for group key `"val1"` (line 536-538) but evaluates `"group_key"` (line 548), so the fingerprints differ (`<id>:val1` vs `<id>:group_key`) and the test still passes. Likewise, in `test_state_results_multi_group`, `occurrence` and `occurrence_2` are equal to each other, and so are `event_data` and `event_data_2`. The `assert_has_calls(..., any_order=True)` (line 206-222) therefore cannot tell group_1's occurrence from group_2's. Derive the id from the group key in the mock (e.g. a hash of the fingerprint), or compare `fingerprint` and `initial_issue_priority` explicitly. Then fix the `"val1"`/`"group_key"` mismatch.

Docstring still says evaluate returns a list

`evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`".

Monitor context returns the raw config, so the `schedule_type` display label is never used

`get_monitor_environment_context` makes a copy of the config at line 160 and puts the display label for `schedule_type` into that copy at line 162. Line 168 then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the copy, so the copy is thrown away and the event's monitor context still carries the integer `schedule_type`. The bug already existed and the move kept it as it was. Since the function now lives in its own module, this is an easy place to fix it: `"config": config,`. The serializer does the same transformation and uses its copy correctly (`src/sentry/monitors/serializers.py:240-242`).

`queued` default is set once, when the module is imported

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs a single time, when the class is defined. Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` (including every one from `from_integration`) then carries the worker process's import time, not the time the assignment was queued. The field is wrong from the start and will mislead anyone who later reads it for ordering or staleness. Use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. `test_to_dict` only checks that `queued` is not None, so it cannot catch this.

No test covers the deassign path when the source integration matches

Only `assign` is tested with a matching `assignment_source`. `deassign` got the same new parameter and is called that way from `sync_group_assignee_inbound` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:96-99), but no test checks that an inbound unassign skips outbound sync to the same integration. Nothing checks either that a *different* integration still gets the outbound sync, which is the other half of the claim in `should_sync`'s comment.

`assignment_source` added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` but nothing passes it

No caller in this PR passes `assignment_source` to `sync_status_outbound`, and subclasses already take `**kwargs`. So this signature change has no effect and suggests status-sync cycle prevention that doesn't exist yet. Either drop it or wire it through in the PR that uses it.

Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned pool; after a rebalance every message is dropped and its offset committed

The factory builds one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and hands the same instance to every strategy it creates (result_consumer.py:254-259). On a partition revocation Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy. `close()` then calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down every queue and stops every worker. `factory.queue_pool` is still set, so the next `create_with_partitions` passes `assert self.queue_pool is not None` and builds a new strategy on the dead pool. From then on, each `submit` calls `add_offset` and then `work_queue.put`, and the put raises `queue.ShutDown`. The `except Exception` at line 317 catches that, logs it, and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop commits it. The result is that every result after the first rebalance is skipped but still committed. That's silent data loss for uptime results. Fix: the strategy shouldn't shut down a pool it doesn't own. Either create the pool per strategy, or leave pool shutdown to `factory.shutdown()` only. On revoke, drain or clear the pool's state for the revoked partitions instead.

Arroyo `commit` is called from a background thread, including for partitions that may have been revoked

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls Arroyo's `Commit` callable (result_consumer.py:249-252). Every other strategy in this file calls `commit` from the consumer thread, inside `submit`/`poll`. Arroyo's StreamProcessor stores pending commit offsets in plain state and doesn't lock it, so this commit races with the main loop. Nothing in `OffsetTracker` clears revoked partitions either: after a revoke, offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns can still be committed and can overwrite the new owner's progress. Collect the committable offsets in the tracker and call `commit` from `poll()` on the consumer thread instead.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring

`queue.Queue()` is created with no `maxsize`, so `put` at line 212 never blocks. The strategy keeps accepting messages from Kafka as fast as the consumer can poll, no matter how far the workers fall behind. Under a processing slowdown (DB latency, a slow subscription) memory grows without limit until the process is OOM-killed. The docstring at line 253 claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up". Fix: give the queues a `maxsize`, and when they are full, raise `MessageRejected` from `submit` so Arroyo pauses and retries the message.

Shutdown drops queued work and the final commit, and can block for up to about 100s

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting the queues down with `immediate=False`. Workers check that flag at the top of each loop (line 129), so each one exits after its current item and abandons whatever is still queued; the non-immediate drain never happens. `close()` stops the commit thread (line 336) before the pool is drained, so offsets completed in the last second are never committed. Those messages get reprocessed after the restart or rebalance. On top of that, the workers are joined one after another with `timeout=5.0` each, so the worst-case shutdown is `num_queues` × 5s (100s with the default 20), plus 5s for the commit thread. During a rebalance that can exceed the poll interval. Fix: drain first (let the workers empty their queues), then do one final commit, and put a single deadline on the whole join instead of one per worker.

Commits stall permanently on any gap in Kafka offsets

`get_committable_offsets` requires every integer offset in the range to have been seen. Kafka offsets aren't guaranteed to be contiguous: transaction control markers and compaction leave gaps. When the topic has such a gap, `highest_committable` stops before it forever, and commits for that partition stop while `all_offsets` keeps growing. Consider walking the sorted set of seen offsets instead of `range()`.

Racy assertion that the queues are non-empty right after submit

Three worker threads are already running and consuming. They can drain all 10 trivial items before `get_stats()` runs, so `stats["total_items"] > 0` fails intermittently. Block the processor with an Event while the stats are checked.

test_preserves_order_within_group does not check order

The test only asserts `len(self.processed_results) == 5`. It should assert that the results arrive in offset order. Since every message has the same `subscription_id`, that means encoding the offset in the payload and comparing against it. The "concurrent" tests don't check concurrency either. None of the tests covers the close-then-recreate (rebalance) path where the shared pool breaks.

Error-handling test checks for the opposite of its docstring and passes only because the commit tick hasn't fired yet

The docstring says errors must not block commits for other messages. The assertion checks the opposite: that nothing is committed (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). The implementation behaves like the docstring, not the assertion. `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` in `finally` even when the processor raises (`queue_consumer.py:144-149`). So once `_commit_loop` runs (it waits 1.0s per tick, `queue_consumer.py:276`), it commits {partition: 102}, which is 101 + 1 (`result_consumer.py:249-252`). The test leaves its wait loop as soon as both calls have happened, then sleeps 0.2s. That is normally well under 1s after the strategy starts, so the assertion only holds because the commit thread hasn't ticked yet. On a slow CI runner the processing can take longer than a second and the test fails. It also never checks the behaviour the docstring promises. Fix: wait for a commit, then assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

Offset-gap test claims the code never commits past a gap, but the code does so on the next tick

With offsets 100, 102 and 103, the first `get_committable_offsets` returns 100 (commit 101). `mark_committed(100)` then drops 100 from `all_offsets`, leaving {102, 103} (`queue_consumer.py:100-105`). On the next tick, `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) = max(101, 102) = 102`, so 102 and 103 become committable and 104 is committed (`queue_consumer.py:83-96`). The gap is skipped about one second after the first commit. The assertions "Should not commit past the gap" and `last_commit == 101` pass only because the test exits roughly 0.2s after the first commit, before the second tick. The test pins down a guarantee the implementation doesn't provide, and it fails whenever a second tick lands inside the wait window. Decide the intended semantics first. Kafka offsets can legitimately have gaps (compaction, transaction markers), so skipping is arguably correct. Then assert that behaviour across at least two commit ticks.

Graceful-shutdown test only checks `queue_pool is None`; it never checks that queued work was drained

The test submits 5 results and only asserts that `factory.queue_pool` is reset. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` (`queue_consumer.py:233-238`). The worker loop is `while not self.shutdown` (`queue_consumer.py:129`), so a worker can exit with items still in its queue. This test would not notice if those items were dropped. Also, `result_processor` is not mocked here, unlike the sibling tests. The real processor runs on daemon worker threads after `send_result` has left its feature context, against the test's transactional DB. Consider mocking the processor and asserting it was called 5 times after `shutdown()`.

"Concurrent subscriptions" test doesn't test concurrency

The docstring says different subscriptions are processed concurrently, but the test only asserts `call_count == 2`. That duplicates `test_thread_queue_parallel`, and it would pass even if every result ran on a single worker. With `max_workers=2`, the two subscription IDs can also hash to the same queue (`hash(group_key) % num_queues`, `queue_consumer.py:202`). To test concurrency, block the first call on an Event and assert that the second call starts anyway. The subscriptions need to be chosen so they land on different queues.

Strategy commit threads and worker threads leak across tests

Each test calls only `factory.shutdown()`. Nothing calls `close()` on the returned `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, so its `_commit_loop` thread keeps running for the rest of the test session, polling every second (`queue_consumer.py:270-276`, `335-338`). `factory.shutdown()` also isn't in a `finally`, so when an assertion fails, the worker threads leak too. Call `consumer.close()` (or `consumer.join()`) and `factory.shutdown()` in a `try/finally` or `addCleanup`.

Kafka test: `KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES` has no effect, `if commits_made` is redundant, and the verify consumer leaks on failure

`StreamProcessor` is given `Topic(test_topic)` directly, so the `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` block doesn't affect what the test exercises. `if commits_made:` is always true once `commit_count >= 1` has passed, so the guard only obscures the assertion. `verify_consumer.close()` runs only when every assertion passes; move it into the `finally` block.

OptimizedCursorPaginator treats a datetime key as a number: every non-empty page returns 500

The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `getattr(item, 'datetime')`. That is a `datetime`, so it raises TypeError the first time `build_cursor` computes a key, which happens on any page with results. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw cursor number, and `build_queryset` (paginator.py:119-126) then compares it to the datetime column. The paginator it replaces, `DateTimePaginator` (paginator.py:233-241), converts in both directions: `strftime('%s.%f') * 1000` and `datetime.fromtimestamp(value/1000)`. So any admin who sends `optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500, and cursors are not compatible between the two paths. Either subclass DateTimePaginator or reuse its key and value conversion.

Negative-offset branch cannot work and is described as reaching data 'beyond normal pagination bounds'

Django QuerySets reject negative slice indices with "Negative indexing is not supported.", so `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `cursor.offset < 0` raises and the request returns a 500. Nothing is paginated. The comments say this is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" and that it "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", which describes an intent to bypass bounds. Remove the branch along with `enable_advanced_features`, and reject negative offsets in cursor parsing with a 400.

BasePaginator change keeps negative offsets for prev cursors, and its comment is wrong

Every paginator that inherits `BasePaginator.get_result` is affected. With `is_prev` set, a client-supplied negative offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-5:1`) still reaches `queryset[offset:stop]`, and Django raises on negative indexing, so the request returns a 500 instead of a 400. Before this change both directions raised the same way. Now only next cursors are clamped. The comment saying "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is false. Clamp in both directions, or raise `BadPaginationError` for `offset < 0`; `paginate` turns that into a ParseError (base.py:540-541).

`organization_context.member` can be None, and `is_superuser` ignores whether superuser mode is active

For a non-superuser request with no org membership, `organization_context.member` is None, and `.has_global_access` raises AttributeError (I did not confirm that OrganizationAuditPermission lets such requests through, e.g. staff). The check also runs for every request, before `use_optimized` is tested. Evaluate it only when `use_optimized` is true and guard against None. Elsewhere Sentry checks `is_active_superuser(request)` rather than `request.user.is_superuser`. This only matters as long as the optimized path is kept (see the paginator findings).

Switching set to sorted-set breaks keys already in Redis during rollout (WRONGTYPE)

Before this change, `span-buf:s:*` keys were Redis sets (SADD/SSCAN). After deploy, `zadd` here, `zcard`/`zunionstore` in add-buffer.lua:46-53, and `zscan` at buffer.py:434 all fail with WRONGTYPE on any segment key written by the old code, until those keys expire (`set_timeout`/redis_ttl). An error in the pipeline makes `p.execute()` raise, so the consumer can crash-loop on those batches and the buffered segments are lost. Either use a new key prefix for the zset keys or handle the migration explicitly.

Oversized segments are now truncated silently, with no metric or log

Before this change, segments over `max_segment_spans` were dropped with the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log. Now `zpopmin` throws away the spans with the earliest end timestamps, and nothing records that it happened, so downstream sees incomplete segments with no signal. The limit of 1000 is also hard-coded here, while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (buffer.py:150,158) is now never read: it is dead config, and it no longer controls the limit. Pass the limit as an ARGV, and emit a metric or a return value when spans are evicted. Note too that `zunionstore` defaults to SUM, so a duplicate payload ends up with a doubled score.

No test for the new 1000-span eviction or for OptimizedCursorPaginator

The test changes only add `end_timestamp_precise` to fixtures, all with the same value. No test covers a segment larger than 1000 spans, the order in which spans are evicted, or the new audit-log `optimized_pagination` path. A single endpoint test with that flag would have caught the datetime TypeError.

Negated query `!event.type:error` counts as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` does a plain substring check, so `!event.type:error` (every event *except* errors), `event.type:errors_foo`, or `message:"event.type:error"` all return True. On the discover dataset this applies `sum(sample_weight)` to queries that are mostly transactions. Transactions have no sample weight, so their counts come back as 0 or wrong, and nothing tells the user. Parse the query with the event-search parser, or at least reject a negated term, before you treat it as error-focused.

Hard-coded `as count` alias breaks `transformAliasToInputFormat=1`

The rewritten column always carries the alias `count`. The response serializer looks the value up by `resolve_axis_column(query_columns[0], ...)` (src/sentry/api/bases/organization_events.py:65-78). That gives `count` by default, but it returns the original `count()` when `transformAliasToInputFormat=1` (line 75-76). For those requests on allowlisted projects, the series key no longer matches the result column, so the chart shows empty or zero buckets and no error is raised. One option is to alias to `resolve_axis_column(column, ...)` of the original column; another is to keep the original column name as the alias.

60s eligibility cache has no working invalidation

The comment on lines 50-53 says the allowlist is read fresh each time, but the result is cached for 60 seconds. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere: the option system has no hook that calls it, and it would need every org/project-set combination to work anyway. So after the allowlist changes, counts flip between upsampled and raw for up to a minute. A single `options.get` call is cheap, so you could drop the cache, or else remove the dead invalidator and correct the docstrings.

What does `sum(sample_weight)` give for events without a sample weight?

The comments say the schema guarantees `sample_weight` for every event in an allowlisted project. Events stored before the project was allowlisted, or sent by SDKs that set no client sample rate, may have a NULL `sample_weight`. `sum` skips NULLs, so those events would drop out of the count silently. Is there a default of 1 in the storage schema? If not, `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` would keep raw counts correct.

Stray gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

This PR adds a submodule entry (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`), and the repository has no `.gitmodules`. It looks like an accidentally committed nested checkout, and it will confuse clones and CI. Remove it from the PR.

Eligibility check uses `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`, and RPC branch is dead

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset`, which the dashboard split factory sets to `errors` when the request dataset is `discover`. The check still passes the outer `dataset`, so a split errors query only gets upsampled if the user's query literally contains `event.type:error`. Separately, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for spans_rpc and ourlogs, so the transform in the `use_rpc` branch (lines 275-277) never runs. The `should_upsample`/`upsampling_enabled` duplication and the comments about "query optimization" don't describe what the code does.

Test creates the organization with `Organization.objects.create`

CLAUDE.md (Common Gotchas #7) says to use the `self.create_*` helpers, not direct model creation. Use `self.create_organization(...)`.

No test for negated queries or the cached path

`test_is_error_focused_query` doesn't cover `!event.type:error`, which currently returns True. Nothing tests `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself, including its caching. The endpoint tests don't cover `transformAliasToInputFormat=1`, multiple yAxis values, or topEvents with upsampling.

Denial-cache test would pass without the denial cache

The comment says this cache entry grants access "to prove this is not checked", but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. `checkPermission` only allows on a truthy value (`scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)]`, service.go:558), so this entry denies. The DB fallback then uses the empty `fakeStore` from `setupService` (service_test.go:1328) and denies too. If you removed the `permDenialCache` short-circuit (service.go:116-121), `resp.Allowed` would still be false, so the test never exercises the code it is named after. Set the value to `true`, or point the store at a permission that grants dash1, so the test fails without the denial-cache check.

Denial cache key is ambiguous when names contain `_`

`name` and `parent` are joined with `_`, and resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores. So `name="a", parent="b_c"` and `name="a_b", parent="c"` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource can then deny a different resource for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s), and nothing logs it. The collision can only cause false denials, never false grants. A separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefixing the parts, would remove the ambiguity.

Denial cache undoes the new fallback-on-cached-deny for repeated checks

The new Check flow goes to the DB when the cached permissions deny (service.go:123-139), so a freshly granted permission is seen right away (the "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" test). After the first denial, though, `permDenialCache` is set for `shortCacheTTL` (30s, service.go:32). Every later check for the same user, action, name and folder then short-circuits to deny at service.go:117 without looking at the permission cache or the DB. A user who was just granted access and retries keeps getting denied for up to 30s. That is about the same staleness as before the change, so this is not a regression, but the asymmetry is worth deciding on deliberately. For example, a shorter TTL for denials, or a comment explaining the trade-off.

`cacheHit` field and its branches are now dead

The only case with `cacheHit: true` was removed, and `getUserPermissions` no longer reads the permission cache. So `cacheHit` is always false, and the branches at lines 367-369 and 388-390 never run. Remove the field and those branches.

KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` in its metadata

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration row has a `sender`. `build_integration` only sets it when `state` has a `sender` (integration.py:376-377). Only the installation webhook passes one (webhook.py:202-209). An Integration created through this pipeline has no `sender`; `test_basic_flow` asserts exactly that metadata (test_integration.py:303-310). `installation.py:44` already guards against a missing `sender`. If an org removes the integration in Sentry, its OrganizationIntegration goes away but the Integration row stays ACTIVE. Reinstalling the same GitHub installation then reaches this line and fails with a 500 instead of an error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide on purpose what should happen when the sender is unknown.

Network and HTTP errors in the OAuth exchange are not handled and become a 500

`safe_urlopen` (line 423) runs outside the `try`, so a connection error or timeout escapes. `get_user_info` calls `resp.raise_for_status()` (identity/github/provider.py:16), so a revoked token or a 401/5xx from `api.github.com/user` raises `HTTPError`, and nothing catches it. In both cases the user gets a server error inside the install popup instead of the `github-integration-failed.html` page, which posts a failure to `window.opener`. Catch these errors and return `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

The installer check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The new check that the authenticated GitHub user matches the installer only runs when an Integration already exists (lines 493-505). If the installation webhook has not been processed yet, `Integration.DoesNotExist` goes straight to `next_step()`. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app's credentials and links it to the current org, and no sender is ever compared. Anyone who knows an `installation_id` before the webhook lands can still claim it. Consider checking the sender from `get_installation_info` (or the webhook state) on this path as well.

`redirect_uri` goes into the authorize URL without URL-encoding

The authorize URL is built with an f-string, so `redirect_uri` (an absolute URL that contains `:` and `/`) is not encoded. That works today only because the path has no `?`, `&` or `#`. Building the query with `urlencode({...})` would be more robust. The test at test_integration.py:233-236 asserts the exact unencoded string, so it would need updating too.

`test_installation_not_found` no longer tests a missing installation

The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the pipeline signature. The request fails at the state check (integration.py:412-413) and returns the default "Invalid installation request.". It never reaches `build_integration`'s 404 handling (integration.py:354-356), so the 404 stub is unused and the "The GitHub installation could not be found." path has lost its coverage. Send the correct state through the OAuth step and keep asserting the not-found message.

Cleanup removes the literal alias "alias", not the IDPs the test created

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` registers a removal of an IDP named `"alias"`, which never exists. The 20 IDPs created in the loop (`"idp-alias-" + i`) and `idp-alias-20` (line 425) never get removed by these cleanups. Capture the alias, e.g. `String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; ... get(alias)::remove`. Line 425 has the same problem.

Changing the shared login predicate also changes the base IdentityProviderBean's federated-IDP list

`getLoginPredicate()` is also what `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()` returns (services/.../IdentityProviderBean.java:225-227), and `getFederatedIdentityProviders` filters on it (line 213). `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` already adds its own org/public check, so nothing changes there. But the base bean (used when organizations are off) now hides a user's linked IDP if it still has an `organizationId` and isn't `BROKER_PUBLIC`. For example, IDPs that were linked to orgs before the feature was turned off would disappear. If the cache only needs this clause for its invalidation decisions, you could add it to a cache-local predicate and leave the public SPI predicate alone.

remove() now always hits the database for the IDP, even when it is cached

Before this change, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` ran only when the alias key was invalid. Now it runs on every remove, even when the `else` branch already has `cached.getIdentityProvider()`. You could use the cached model (or `getByAlias`) for the login-invalidation check and only fall back to the delegate when nothing is cached. The cost is small: one extra query per removal.

enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, so the feature-flag check does nothing

Both branches return `false`, so the `IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` call (line 195) has no effect, and the inverted `enabled := !...` name points the wrong way. Turning on `sqlExpressions` still gives "sqlExpressions is not implemented", which is what the PR wants. But a reader will take this for a flag gate with a bug in it. Either drop the helper and return the error directly in `case QueryTypeSQL` (with a comment saying SQL expressions are disabled until a new engine lands), or write it as `return false // disabled: no SQL engine`.

The legacy node path is not gated and reports a misleading 'invalid sql' error

Only `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` checks `enableSqlExpressions`. The legacy `TypeSQL` branch in `pkg/expr/nodes.go:159-160` calls `UnmarshalSQLCommand` → `NewSQLCommand` → `sql.TablesList`, which now always fails because the stub `RunCommands` returns "not implemented". The user gets the BadRequest `sql-invalid-sql` / "error reading SQL command", and a Warn "invalid sql query" is logged, which suggests their SQL is malformed. Consider returning the same "sqlExpressions is not implemented" error early in `NewSQLCommand` or `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, so both paths fail the same way and the message is accurate.

DB.TablesList stub is unused

Nothing calls the `TablesList` method on `DB`. The only callers use the package-level `sql.TablesList` (`pkg/expr/sql_command.go:30`, `pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go`), and that function goes through `RunCommands`. The method sits next to the package function of the same name, which is confusing. Remove it unless a planned interface needs it.

No second cache check after taking the write lock

When the cache is still empty (first requests after startup, or after a load that failed), every caller that got `nil` under the RLock (41-43) waits on `Lock()` here. Each one then reads and parses `assets-manifest.json` again, one after another. Nothing checks whether an earlier holder has already filled the cache. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` right after line 49 and returning early would make the startup herd parse the manifest only once. This doesn't affect correctness: the result is the same either way.

Debug logging left in at Error level, including every batch's full ID list

Each batch callback logs twice with `r.log.Error`: once before the delete (534, 554, 576) and once after (537, 557, 579). The first call also includes the whole `ids` slice. That slice holds up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` IDs, and the new test sets that to 32767. `untilDoneOrCancelled` (643-660) always runs one last batch that returns 0, so these Error lines fire on every cleanup cycle even when there is nothing to delete. That covers MaxAge and MaxCount for each annotation type, plus the tag cleanup. Together with the ticker going down to 1 minute in `cleanup.go:77`, this puts a steady stream of false error-level logs into production logs and alerting. The `"err", err` field at 534/554/576 is always nil because the error was checked just above. Remove these lines, or lower them to Debug and log only counts.

Cleanup ticker cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute; looks like a leftover from debugging

This ticker drives all eight cleanup jobs (lines 96-105), not only annotations: tmp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs and query history. Every Grafana instance would now run all of them 10× as often. The per-run timeout is still `9 * time.Minute` (line 89), which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval and no longer matches. Nothing in the PR description explains the change. Restore `time.Minute * 10`, or make the interval a config setting and keep the timeout in line with it.

Building the inline ID list with repeated Sprintf is quadratic

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole growing string on every iteration. This path only runs when the batch size is above 999, so the batch can hold tens of thousands of IDs (the test uses 32767), and that is O(n²) copying per batch. Use a `strings.Builder` with `strconv.AppendInt`, or `strings.Join` over the formatted IDs.

"running the max count delete again" no longer runs anything again

Each subtest now creates its own data (line 116) and wipes the tables afterwards (120-127). This case therefore just inserts 9 annotations (3 per type) and checks that MaxCount=3 deletes nothing. The name still describes the old behaviour, where it ran a second time over the previous case's leftover state. That idempotence check is gone. Rename the case, or run `cleaner.Run` twice in one subtest so it still tests a second run.

Background legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the handler returns

All four goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their 10s timeout as a child of the request `ctx`. `Create`/`Update`/... then return right away. The HTTP server cancels the request context once the handler finishes, and that cancels the child context too, so the legacy write races against cancellation and often gets aborted. Legacy storage then drifts from unified storage with nothing to show for it. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the logger and identity values), then apply the timeout to that.

Failed legacy writes are no longer logged

The old code logged every legacy failure (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not update object in legacy store`, ...). The goroutines now only call `recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...)` and throw the error away (l.56, l.113, l.140, l.165). If a legacy write fails or times out, no log line names the object or the cause. Add `log.Error(err, ...)` in each goroutine.

The branch at lines 144-146 drops the first label of both hosts and compares the rest. On a forum at `forum.co.uk`, the website `http://evil.co.uk/whatever` matches (`co.uk` == `co.uk`), so its full path is shown as if it were on the same site. No test for the sibling-subdomain branch, a blank website, or a TL0-anonymous viewer

The specs cover the exact-match, unrelated-host and parent-domain branches. They don't cover the `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` branch (line 144-146), a website with no host (e.g. `example.com` without a scheme, where `URI(...).host` is nil), or `website_name` being omitted for a TL0 user seen as anonymous.
